subject: history_social
passage: In the late Middle Ages, enormous shoals of herring gathered each autumn off the coast of Scania, at the southern tip of what is now Sweden, and fishermen from around the Baltic Sea came to catch them. Herring spoils within a day or two unless it is packed in salt, and the Scania shore had no salt of its own. The nearest large supply was the salt works at Lüneburg, in northern Germany, whose output reached the fishing grounds by way of the port of Lübeck. Lübeck's merchants owned few fishing boats, yet contemporary records show them setting the terms on which much of the Scania catch was sold. Historian Pieter de Vries argues that this influence is best explained by the fact that ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the Scania fishery would have been far more profitable if salt had been produced on the Scania shore.
choices.B: merchants who controlled salt could dictate the price of every good traded around the Baltic Sea.
choices.C: Lübeck's merchants caught most of the Scania herring themselves and so could set their own prices.
choices.D: whoever controlled the supply of salt controlled whether the catch could be preserved at all.

explanation.why: Two facts must be combined: herring is worthless unless salted within a day or two, and the only large supply of salt reached Scania through Lübeck. Fishermen therefore depended on Lübeck's merchants for the one thing that made their catch worth having, which explains the merchants' power over its sale.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never discusses the profits of the fishery or what local salt would have changed; it asks why Lübeck's merchants had influence.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text explains influence over one trade that depended on salt; it says nothing about other goods.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says Lübeck's merchants owned few fishing boats; their power came from something other than catching the fish.
explanation.D: Correct. Without salt the herring spoiled within days, and the salt came through Lübeck, so Lübeck's merchants held the key to the whole trade even without boats of their own.
